simplified_idea: Researchers used new methods to challenge the idea that science is always neutral and unbiased. These studies introduced new ways to look critically at how scientific work is actually done.

The author argues that scientific research about sex and gender is often influenced by cultural stereotypes. This shows that science is not always neutral and can be shaped by social ideas about men and women.

The author argues that scientific research is never truly neutral because it is always shaped by political views and social assumptions. Feminist STS shows that politics was already part of science, rather than being something new that was added to it.
The author will use examples of how scientific views on sex and gender can affect politics to show how research and politics are connected.

The author explains that separating biological sex from social gender roles helps people question why women are often expected to do more housework. This distinction shows that social roles are not naturally determined by biology.

People value work done by men more than work done by women. Although some thinkers tried to change this by showing that 'feminine' tasks are important, they failed. This failure accidentally made people believe that women are naturally meant to do less important work than men.

Judith Butler argues that we should not treat sex and gender as separate things because doing so makes biology seem like the cause of gender, which maintains unfair power structures. She also explains that we cannot understand the human body without considering the culture and society it exists in.
